authoring.question: q-117485
authoring.value:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}9y-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ y(9-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013903/assets/bbcf218e7b6181c861ba4c804357cc53ae6004453914259a9fe98ad5f09ac4d4.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=9y-{y}^{3}$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=0$ to $y=3.$ 
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(9y-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =9\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{3}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =9\cdot (\frac{(3)^{2}}{2}-0)-(\frac{(3)^{4}}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{81}{2}-\frac{81}{4} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

authoring.value:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{16}{y}^{5}-3y & =0 \\ \frac{3}{16}y({y}^{4}-16) & =0 \\ \frac{3}{16}y({y}^{2}-4)({y}^{2}+4) & =0 \\ \frac{3}{16}y(y-2)(y+2)({y}^{2}+4) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14032052/assets/03737836a352eafaf486e7e5f71d882ac39715e788a0c9113eb809b185584bdc.png)

We want the area between the curve $x=\frac{3}{16}{y}^{5}-3y$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-2$ to $y=0.$
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}(\frac{3}{16}{y}^{5}-3y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{16}{\int }_{-2}^{0}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y-3{\int }_{-2}^{0}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{y}^{6}\,{|}_{-2}^{0}-\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}(0-(-64))-\frac{3}{2}(0-4) \\  & =-2+6 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

authoring.question: e-426
authoring.value:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013903/assets/f2a29faeb9db8e622a21a0e77bea911960a5c64d87a2c900ecd0c0213b2e4bce.png)

We want the area between the curve $x=y^2-4$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=-2$ to $y=2.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}({y}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-8{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-8y{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2(\frac{8}{3}-0)-8(2-0) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-16 \\  & =-\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $\left|-\dfrac{32}{3}\right| = \dfrac{32}{3}.$
